extmeta.Categories: Portable Antiquities Scheme|Images uploaded by Fæ|Portable Antiquities Scheme, LON|Tiles in the Portable Antiquities Scheme|Files with coordinates missing SDC location of creation (51° N, 1° W)|Encaustic tiles in the United Kingdom
extmeta.ImageDescription:
A Medieval incomplete ceramic glazed floor tile (1350s-1390s). The tile is decorated with a two-tone pattern in white slip against a red background. The pattern comprises a central flower motif with five petals with a circular border. In each corner there is another five petalled flower within a semi-circular border; this border is broken and the broken spur protrudes in the central circular border. Traces of glaze remain. Some of the tile and the pattern are missing.

Jackie Keily suggested it was produced in Penn, Buckinghamshire.

Identification by Jackie Keily, Curator, Museum of London.

Dimensions: Thickness: 21.09mm; Weight: 172.63g.

extmeta.Artist: Museum of London, Kate Sumnall, 2009-12-21 11:39:48
extmeta.ImageDescription:
A fragment of Roman ceramic roof tile (tegula) (43-410 AD). The fragment consists of part of the wall of a Roman tegula tile, the lower section of the overlapping Roman roof tile pattern in which curved imbrex tiles were laid over the adjoining walls of a row of tegulae underneath. The upper edge of this tegula wall is the only side of the fragment that remains complete; the other three edges are broken. The tile has been hand built from a buff, highly-fired stoneware fabric with quartz tempering. One side of the tile fragment has a large area of concretion with gritty inclusions. 
Dimensions: weight: 176.03g.

extmeta.Artist: Birmingham Museums Trust, Teresa Gilmore, 2010-08-04 10:01:08
extmeta.ImageDescription:
A fragment of a line impressed ceramic floor tile, of later medieval dating (13th to 15th Centuries AD).

Approximately 40% of the tile is present and consists of a orangey red oxidised ceramic tile with a light brown transparent glaze with a line impressed design. The glaze extends down the original edges. The floor tile would probably have been triangular (corner) in shape. Three original edges survive, the central diagonal one indicates that the tile was originally made as a square and designed to be broken into two to create two triangular tiles.

The design present consists of three semi circles with a five petalled flower in the centre of the semi circles. The closest line to the flower appears to have part of a leaf and it spirals into the flower, suggesting it was meant to be the stem. The design would have been imprinted onto the wet tile using a wooden stamp.

The tile measures 96.92mm in length, 68.63mm in width and 22.83mm thick. It weighs 207.0 grams.

title: File:Medieval foor finial tile, horse's head, as broken (FindID 425214).jpg

extmeta.ObjectName: Medieval foor finial tile, horse's head, as broken
extmeta.Categories: Portable Antiquities Scheme|Images uploaded by Fæ|Figurines in the Portable Antiquities Scheme|Portable Antiquities Scheme, DENO|Tiles in the Portable Antiquities Scheme|Files with coordinates missing SDC location of creation (52° N, 2° W)
extmeta.Artist: Derby Museums Trust, Rachel Atherton, 2011-01-24 10:13:12
extmeta.ImageDescription:
Medieval pottery figurine in the form of a stylised horse's head/neck. Modelled in the round with striations indicating the mane on the neck and forehead; the head is broken away from the body but is present, although damaged at the ears, one eye and along the snout; the surviving eye is formed by an impressed ring and dot - the eye is orange coloured and appears to have been applied separately. A short applied strip on the left side of the neck, behind the mane, perhaps indicates the bridle/reins. Degraded yellow-green glaze. Coarse very sandy fabric with reduced-fired grey core and oxidised-fired skin varying cream and orange; abundant angular white quartz sand inclusions (0.5mm-3mm) giving pimply appearence to surface. In two fragments - the head is broken away from the neck. Length (from the break at the neck to the forehead) 104mm, width (throat to mane) 80mm, thickness at base of neck 35mm, weight 182.8g + 48.1g.

This is probably a fragment of a roof-finial tile, or possibly an aquamanile or other fancy pottery vessel fragment. The lack of a pouring spout through the head, and the coarseness of the fabric, perhaps preclude this from being an aquamanile / vessel.

Blair & Ramsay, 1991 ("English Medieval Industries: craftsmen, techniques, products", Continuum) write 'Finials of stone, wood or pottery were used from the 11th century onwards to decorate the gable and the ridges of medieval roofs. Some were in the form of spikes, other like human faces, and some represented standing animals such as horses, bears, dragons or lions.' They note that ceramic tililng was first used during the medieval period in England during the 12th century, and that 'the earliest archaeological and documentary evidence for ridge tiles dates from the 13th century'.

extmeta.ObjectName: Medieval inlaid ceramic floor tile
extmeta.Categories: Portable Antiquities Scheme|Images uploaded by Fæ|Portable Antiquities Scheme, SOM|Files with coordinates missing SDC location of creation (50° N, 4° W)
extmeta.Artist: The Portable Antiquities Scheme, Edward Caswell, 2019-06-17 11:29:17
extmeta.ImageDescription:
One inlaid ceramic floor tile of Medieval date, similar to 'Stabbed Wessex' types dating to 1280 to 1350, found as part of a larger group. The tile has parts of two complete edges and two broken sides, no edge is complete so the original size is unclear. The tile has a heavily reduced interior which appears hard and with a bright orange oxidised surface. The front is decorated with inlaid white clay with traces of glaze remaining in places. The design is mostly worn, the clearest part remaining is of a quadruped, probably a dog walking left with front legs split and straight back legs and tail raised, the head is missing to a break. The dogs feet are adjacent to the complete edge suggesting this is part of a larger design. Further white inlay remains to the right of the dog but it is unclear what the traces show, possibly a border, foliage or even a hunter as such dogs are often shown as part of hunting scenes.

The sides are angled inwards so the back is smaller than the front. The back has widely by irregularly scattered stabbed keying holes. The holes are circular and conical, narrowing gradually but consistently to the rounded tips, visible in the break. Due to the reduced fabric and mortar remains inclusions are hard to identify clearly but seem to include common very fine sand.

The tile measures 109.7mm long, 107.3mm wide, 23.7mm thick and weighs 486 grams.

The fabric and keying form may suggest the 'Stabbed Wessex' group found across central southern England in the late 13th to mid 14th century. However it has not been possible to compare this example directly to any from the group. Although hunting scenes are known in churches from this group (Lowe, 2003 p17-18) and include examples where the dog is 'walking' directly on the edge the exact design has not yet been paralleled. Wessex School material is found across Somerset and Dorset although this would be on the edge of the distribution (Lowe 2003, p10). The earliest recorded incumbent at Burlescombe is in the earlt 14th cnetury, although the present church is mainly later in fabric, so it is possible this dates from the 14th century.

The tile was found, with others recorded as SOM-6B93EE, <a href="https://finds.org.uk/database/artefacts/record/id/958570">SOM-6BDD93</a> and <a href="https://finds.org.uk/database/artefacts/record/id/958574">SOM-6C2FC5</a>, under the floor of the nave of Burlescombe church during recent renovations. They had been used to support floor beams put in place in the extensive 1843 refurbishment and are almost certainly remnants of earlier decorative schemes.

extmeta.Artist: Birmingham Museums Trust, Tom Brindle, 2010-09-13 11:07:06
extmeta.ImageDescription:
Two ceramic tiles. One is probably a floor tile, the other is less certain and may possibly be a roof tile.

The floor tile is sub-square in shape although it may be broken on one edge. It measures 84.5 mm long and 83 mm wide and is 20.5 mm thick. It weighs 244.5 grams. It is undecorated.

The other tile is incomplete and measures 99 mm long, 70 mm wide and 13 mm thick. It weighs 83.9 grams. It is also undecorated.

Because of their lack of decoration the tiles are difficult to date. Finds recovered from the same location include medieval 14th century floor tile, 14th century pottery and 17th to 18th century pottery. A broad date range, from the medieval to post-medieval period is therefore suggested.
